                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| 12.3                                            | The first provider is a **Google Flights scraper**, and the seam for a second one exists before the second one does.                                                                                                                                                                                                              | It is the only free source that returns the full itinerary list with carrier and departure time, which is the granularity the feature is for. Measured from a residential address: plain `httpx` with a browser User-Agent answered 200 on LIM-CUZ, LIM-SCL, LIM-MIA and LIM-MAD with no consent page. It is also the piece most likely to break, so `adapters/fares/registry` exists from the first commit rather than after the first breakage.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| 12.4                                            | Parse drift is a **typed error**, never an empty result.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | The payload is an untagged array read by position. When Google renumbers it the request still succeeds and the page still parses — it simply yields nothing, which is indistinguishable from a quiet week on a route. `parse-drift` separates "we can no longer read this" from `no-offers`, which is Google saying there are no flights. Same reasoning applied to the archive: every line unreadable is logged as an error, not a warning. JSONL under `.local-data/fares/`, one file per route.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `BarCache` replaces a whole series on every write, which is right when upstream is the authority and our copy is a convenience. Here we are the authority — nobody else remembers what LIM-SCL cost on a Tuesday — so a write that replaces is a write that destroys. Recorded in ADR 0002 because it departs from the store the data plane already had. | 12.6                                            | A watched route is a route **and a departure date**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | The price of "LIM to SCL" is not a thing; the price of "LIM to SCL on 16 October" is. One archive file holds every date ever watched for a pair, so the series is filtered by departure before it is charted — otherwise the step between an October fare and a December one is drawn as a price movement. Attaching one would be an invention that later arithmetic takes seriously, and parsing it in the browser would move a 00:15 Lima departure by the reader's own distance from Lima. Rendered as text, end to end. USD rather than PEN because a history is read across months and a local-currency series moves when the exchange rate moves, which looks exactly like a fare change and is not one. Cloud is deferred, not merely unbuilt.                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Google fingerprints datacenter addresses — the concern 8.4 recorded and 10.6 built a probe for, arriving here as a hard constraint rather than a suspicion. A Cloud Run job would meet a consent wall, so moving the schedule to GCP means changing the provider first (AIR-02). The collector is a stateless command so that move is a host change and not a rewrite. Reader and writer are genuinely different halves of one format, so they share a file and a docstring. import features, and there is no zoom window here to share. Nothing about the token is prefixed `VITE_`: that prefix is what ships a value to the browser. |
| 12.14                                           | Travelpayouts was **measured and dropped**. One provider, and the seam stays.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Built, exercised against a real token, and closed unmerged on 2026-08-18 — the head-to-head is why. Over 15 route-dates it answered 5 to the scraper's 15, and nothing at all at +120 days. Where both answered, its price differed by -30.0%, -18.4%, -8.3%, -8.0% and +5.5%, almost always for a different carrier at a different hour, because it serves a days-old cache of other people's searches. A fallback that draws a 30% drop that never happened is not a worse observation than a gap, it is a false one. The registry keeps its seam; what it does not keep is a second answer nobody can reconcile with the first. | 12.15                                           | The price is read **to the cent**, out of the token beside the rounded one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `itinerary[1][0][1]` is what the page prints. The base64 token next to it carries `{units, decimals, currency}` — 5982, 2, USD for a fare printed as 60. Measured 2026-08-18: two LIM-CUZ offers both displaying 64 were 63.34 and 63.36, so rounding merges distinct fares in the one file whose job is noticing when a fare moves. The rounded integer stays as the fallback, because a token we cannot read should cost precision and not the observation. | 12.16                                           | A snapshot is written **only when something changed**; a heartbeat is written **every time**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Measured 2026-08-18 on real snapshots: two taken 23 seconds apart were identical, two taken 8 minutes apart were identical, and the first change appeared across 11.5 hours where 3 of 25 flights moved. Four of five snapshots were pure duplicates. Polling every half hour and writing every time would cost 110 MB per route per year of copies, in a file read by scanning it — exactly the case ADR 0002 flagged as not holding up. The heartbeat is not optional: without it a quiet week and a dead collector leave the same trace, and a series whose gaps are ambiguous is a series nobody should trust. | 12.17                                           | Cadence follows **how far away the departure is**, and the bounds come from the endpoint.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | At 14 days out a fare moved on 27% of days by a median 14%; at 150 days it moved on 22% of days by 1.7% — the same frequency carrying a twentieth of the news. So 30 minutes near, daily far, configurable in between. The floor is 15 minutes because nothing was ever observed to change faster; the ceiling is 24 hours because slower is coarser than the free history Google already gives away. The daily request budget is the one number here that is a judgement rather than a measurement: the endpoint is unmetered, and the real limit is how much traffic one address can send before it stops being answered, which is unknown and deliberately unprobed — finding it costs exactly the asset it protects. It thins to 52 points by +280 days and is gone by +330. This does not overturn 12.2: nobody sells a fare history, and this one is a rolling window that only reaches backwards. But it was being downloaded and thrown away, so a route now starts with two months of context instead of one point. It lives in its own file and is drawn dashed, because it is one rounded integer a day with no airline and no departure time — the same reason 12.14 refused to let a coarser source share a line. Identity held up in practice — 25 of 33 flights kept the same key across a whole day, and every one that did not had genuinely rotated off the board. A flight that leaves stays in the table marked absent, because a departure that stopped being sold is one of the more useful things this archive can report. Before this the repository knew `LIM` only as three letters matching a regular expression. The alternative was a bundled IATA table of 40–60 kB — heavier than the entire map — which would also have needed maintaining. They go to one `airports.json` for the whole archive rather than one per route, because an airport is a fact about the world and LIM appearing in nine watched pairs should not be nine copies that can disagree. This is also the one part of the archive that is genuinely re-fetchable, so it is written whole rather than appended. Escaping all three means passing a blank style, self-hosting the worker and bundling our own geometry, at which point the tile renderer has no tiles and what remains is its arc layer. Measured alternative: 13 kB of code and 39 kB of geometry, no network ever, and every arc is a DOM node a test can query — the same argument 12.12 made for the price chart. `d3-scale` was already a dependency, so `d3-geo` is a sibling rather than a new class of thing. The band is the range of the cheapest fare within the period and the line is its median, chosen over the mean so one collection during a fare glitch cannot drag a week. Candles were considered and rejected: open and close only mean something if you observed at both ends of the period, which write-on-change does not promise, so the shape would claim a precision the data does not have. The provider's baseline stays a separate dashed series for the reason 12.19 already gave — at day granularity it is one rounded integer with no band possible. A CSS transition cannot do this on its own — the node unmounts, and a transition on a mounting node never runs — so it is kept only for the jumps geometry does not cover, a zoom press or a change of projection. Measured over one drag: South America 0.55 → 0.44 → 0.22 → 0.03 → gone, with Oceania coming up the other way. But `countries-110m` already carries a name per shape, so 176 labels cost zero additional bytes — positioned at the largest polygon's centroid, because a whole-shape centroid puts France four degrees out in the Atlantic. A name appears once the ground under it is big enough to hold it, estimated from the projection's local area scale factor (`r²·cos θ` orthographic, `s²·sec²φ` Mercator) rather than by streaming a polygon: checked against `geoPath.area` on six real countries in both projections, within 5%, at one cosine per label. Room alone was not enough — Russia and Brazil have room in the very first frame — so the layer is also gated on zoom, and crosses over with the continents at about 2.2×. | 12.30                                           | The flat map's zoom **multiplies the fit** instead of being capped by it, and the pan clamp covers both axes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | The scale read `min(width / 2π, radius · 0.6)` with the zoom already inside `radius` — and `width / 2π` is exactly the scale that fits 360° of longitude across the frame, so the cap bit at about 1.1× and the flat map stopped zooming there while the globe went on to 8×. With zoom applied to the unzoomed fit instead, the map becomes wider than the frame, which makes sideways worth reaching. Rather than a hard axis lock, the clamp measures the projected sphere on both axes: at the default zoom that still reads as up and down only, because there genuinely is nothing to reach sideways. One frame of slip at 60 Hz is small and entirely visible: the map slides out from under its own labels for as long as the drag lasts. `flushSync` costs the same work undeferred, and only ever runs while a pointer is down. belong to. Colour now says _which_ route and nothing about price — the detail panel says that in words and a number, where there is room. Seven hues evenly around the wheel from the app's own accent, each fitted to the same perceived luminance as that accent (matched to within 0.002) at one moderate saturation, so none outshines the others and only temperature separates them. Emitted as a stride across the wheel rather than around it, which lifts the smallest gap between neighbouring routes from 41 to 113 in RGB. A first hand-picked set failed its own check — amber and copper sat 22 apart. | 12.51                                           | Zoom is **continuous, about the cursor, and has no buttons**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Proportional was not enough, and the first attempt proved it. The factor is exponential in the wheel delta (`exp(-deltaY · 0.002)`, d3-zoom's own constant) — a trackpad reports a few pixels per gesture and a mouse notch about a hundred, so a fixed factor per event gives the trackpad a crawl and the mouse a jump — but applying even the right factor _in full, the instant the event arrives_ is a 22% change in one frame, and 22% in one frame is a step. A tile renderer, which is what mapcn is underneath, sets a **target** and animates towards it. So a notch moves the target and the frame loop eases the scale after it: about 63% of the remaining distance per 70ms, framed in elapsed time so the glide takes the same wall-clock time at 60 Hz and at 144 Hz, snapping at the end because an exponential approach never actually arrives and a scale a thousandth away keeps the loop awake for nothing. One step is applied on the event itself, so the map answers a notch in the frame it arrived in. Zoom lives in a ref, not state — a wheel gesture fires dozens of events and each one was a React render before anything could be drawn; held in a ref the handler writes a number and the frame loop picks it up, the same path a drag takes. Scaling about the middle of the frame slides the thing you are pointing at away exactly when you are trying to reach it, so both projections hold the point under the cursor still: the flat map shifts its pan, and the globe _turns_, because an orthographic has no pan. The bug that cost the most: the correction wrote the new rotation _after_ the fit that used it, so every notch drew one frame of un-anchored zoom — the projections are now refitted before `zoomAbout` returns, and a test pins it. Plus and minus buttons are gone; `+` and `-` on the focused map keep zoom reachable without a wheel. Sized as if empty it contributes nothing, the chart alone sets the row, and `flex: 1 1 0` spends the height that leaves. Hidden stretches count towards it, which is what stops the pattern sticking to the horizon as the globe turns — measured over 21 airports, a route in this map's home view is almost always one drawn path, but 98 of the pairs tried start behind the limb and their one visible run begins part-way along its own arc. Screen length rather than arc-radians because the projection foreshortens hard near the limb and a phase in radians would bunch the dashes up exactly there. The pattern is 10 units (`5 5`, and `7 3` for the open route, which was `7 4` — eleven units under a ten-unit cycle slides back a unit every time round) and travels one whole period per cycle, so the loop has no seam. Measured end to end against the live provider, the press now returns in **6.7 ms** where it used to block for the length of the pass, and what bounds a pass is `daily_request_budget()` — which is what the bound should always have been. One pass runs at a time and a second press is answered with the running one, because the gap paces a single loop and two loops would halve it with nobody deciding to; that was already the honest behaviour and was previously enforced nowhere, so two rows pressed together really did run two loops. `watching` is how a row tells its own pass from somebody else's, and `polling` is settled before the first request so a four-minute pass has a denominator from the start rather than a spinner. Note, unfixed and predating this, that the budget is spent per pass and nothing accumulates spend across passes, so the daily figure the name promises is not actually enforced. Three is what was measured rather than what was hoped for: twelve requests at three seconds and twelve more at two came back clean — no 429, no consent redirect, no `ErrorResponse` — and mean latency **fell** as the gap closed (0.630s at six, 0.421s at three, 0.394s at two), which is a warm connection and the opposite of a throttle. Two was clean too and is deliberately not taken; three is the pace with the most evidence behind it and the unused floor is the margin. What this does not rest on is daily volume, which nobody here has probed — and does not have to, because pacing changes how tightly a day's requests are packed and not how many there are. The scrollbar stays drawn `thin` beside it: the platform's own answer cannot be out of step with its box, and the shadow is the half that survives an overlay scrollbar fading out. The reachability is the other half — the rows hold buttons, so Tab walks in, but that is the only way in; the scroller carries its own tab stop and an accessible name so a reader who is reading rather This module has 177 particular geometries, so **the rings are flattened once at import into `Float64Array` pairs and answered by even-odd ray casting in the longitude/latitude plane.** Against Chile, 8,804 samples: 122 ms spherically, 11 ms as a plain planar ray cast, 1.9 ms once the ring is a typed array — and almost half of the win is the typed arrays rather than the geometry. **A plane is wrong about a sphere in exactly two ways and both are answered rather than accepted.** An edge is a great circle and bows off its chord by `(Δλ)²·sin(2φ)/8`, worst 0.2799° across one of Canada's 9° Arctic edges, so every edge over 1° is cut into pieces along its own arc at import: 10,587 vertices become 12,159, and the disagreements over a 0.5° world grid fall from 44 to 11 across the whole atlas. A polygon can wrap the date line, which Russia's and Fiji's do — answered by moving the seam (`SHIFTED`), not by approximating them, because Russia's box covers every longitude from 41°N up and a spherical fallback there costs 610 vertices per sample over Europe: 36.8 ms against 4.0 for that one view. Antarctica goes round the pole rather than past the seam, is 360° wide on either sheet, and is the one polygon that keeps `geoContains`. **What is left is narrower than the atlas's own error:** over 45,619,200 answers on a 0.5° world grid, 11 differ; over 6,635,705 at 0.05° across the five countries this watchlist flies between, 64 differ and the furthest is 353 m from an outline, against a 1:110m outline that is itself a median of 1.5 to 5.2 km from the 1:10m one drawn over it. Held at the same step, this changes the detected set in 5 of 1,656 views, each by one grid cell on a shared border, and in none of them does a country that would carry a name appear or disappear, or a country change which one holds most of the screen. Eleven canvases at each of two stage sizes are byte-identical before and after.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

The hint — try the country the last sample landed in — carries a zoomed-in view, but a sample over the sea matches no hint and fell through to every box in the atlas, and then to a polygon test for each box that happened to contain it. Chile's box runs from Easter Island to Cape Horn, so half the South Pacific was paying for Chile. The index is 72 by 36 buckets holding 3,354 entries, 758 of them empty, a median non-empty bucket of one shape and a fullest of twelve, so a sample walks one box where it walked 177 and none at all over most of the ocean. Measured on a 1550x460 stage at step 12, toggling only this: 3.3 times over Santiago at 32x, 5.2 times over open Pacific, 3.4 times over central Europe at 3.4x, 3.2 times over Lima at 8x. **It cannot Widening the column was rejected as the same fault with a later trigger: whatever the number is, the next carrier name overflows it. Truncation was rejected outright — `Aerolineas Arg…` reads as the name of an airline and is not one, which is the objection `.report` in `RouteList.module.css` already records. Giving the long figure its own row, or letting it span two columns, were both rejected for spending a whole row on a value that fits in less. Sized by content the six figures ask 735px of the 1252 there are, so a 45-character `Compañía Panameña de Aviación Sociedad Anónima` still lands on one row in full, and past that it folds between its words. The cost is that figures on a wrapped second line no longer sit under those on the first; a label still stands over its own figure, which is the pair a reader follows. Three separate things moved it and none of them is the reader: the board box is a six-figure `<dl>` where there are observations and a one-line “Nothing observed yet” where there are not, 64.2px against 24.2; the header's “Cheapest on 06/12/2026” and “Last look …” lines are there only where a board has been read and a collector has run, and that header is the taller of the two things in the strip's top row, so its four lines _are_ the row's height and two of them come and go, 109.5px against 75.6; and a carrier name long enough to fold takes a second line of value. About 74px of the page below, on every route change. `both-charts-share-one-fixed-box` is the precedent and this is the same move — the box is fixed and what it holds lays out inside it — with `align-content: start` packing the flex lines at the top so a fold spends room the box already had rather than asking for more. It departs from that decision in exactly one respect and does it deliberately: a floor rather than a ceiling. “A floor is half a promise” was right there because chart B exceeded the floor _always and by a known amount_, so a floor left the reflow where it found it; the case that overshoots two lines here is a value at a width the strip has already stacked at, and what a ceiling does to it is paint the overflow outside the border — which is the ink on ink this branch exists to remove, arriving by a different door. Truncating to fit a ceiling was rejected on `.report`'s grounds, which `a-figure-takes-what-it-holds` had already reached: `Aerolineas Arg…` reads as the name of an airline and is not one. **Nothing in `a-figure-takes-what-it-holds` is withdrawn** — a figure is still exactly as wide as its own label and value, the slack is still shared out, and a long name still folds rather than being cut. This only stops that width from deciding a height. The cost, stated plainly: the board box carries a blank line under its five short figures at every width — 24.6px the chart below does not get back — because that line is what the sixth figure folds into, and the strip is a strip precisely because its height is worth arguing over. What is _not_ fixed is width: below the width at which six figures stop fitting on one row the box takes two and is taller, which is the reader resizing their window rather than the data changing under them. Every number here is arithmetic over the rules in `RouteDetail.module.css` at `--font-size-base: 125%` and `reset.css`'s `line-height: 1.5`, not a browser measurement — this branch had no dev server to take one on. It is checked against those same rules in `RouteDetail.test.tsx` rather than asserted, because jsdom lays nothing out and no rendering test can see a height.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

| a-taller-row-is-four-more-routes                | **The first row is 640px of stage rather than 460**, which is ten watched routes without a scrollbar, and the map grows with it rather than holding its old height beside a taller list.                                                                                                                                          | The owner: "aumentar su largo para habilitar espacio para mas rutas y evitar por el momento el uso de barra de desplazamiento". `.stage`'s `min-height` is the only height in that row — the watchlist is sized as if it were empty (12.269) — so the number of routes that fit is set in the map's stylesheet, which is worth saying because it is where nobody would look. Written out: the watchlist spends 156.1px more above its scroller than the map spends above its stage (a head and its margin and the panel's gap, 68.5; the add form, its rule and another gap, 139; against the map's toolbar and 8px column gap, 51.4), and a row is 40.5px — Remove's 38.5 rather than the route button's 35.4, plus the 2px gap the always-present report line costs while empty — with 5px between, so n rows are `45.5n - 5`. At 460 the scroller was 303.9px and held **six** with 35.9 standing, a seventh 9.6px short; at 640 it is 483.9 and holds **ten** with 33.9 standing, an eleventh 11.6px short. Six is exactly what the reader had watched, which is why there was a scrollbar to complain about, and the two figures reproducing that is the check on the whole sum. **Ten was chosen, and the alternatives are worth naming**: eight (550px) gives a list that already has six routes only two rows of headroom, and twelve (730px) makes the first row taller than a 1080p viewport has to spare above the analysis panel's own 34.5rem. Capping the stage at 460 while the list grew was the alternative, and it costs a panel with 180px of nothing under a map and a globe that stayed the size it was, for no gain but the sweep. **What it costs is the settle sweep, and only that.** `countriesInView` walks `ceil((d - 6) / 12)` samples an axis, so the widest stage goes from 129x38 to 136x53 — 4,902 samples to 7,208, up 47% — and the ten views `contains-is-flat-not-spherical` measured at 1.20 to 4.42 ms are 1.76 to 6.50 ms, once, on the frame after a gesture stops, still seven to twelve times cheaper than the 12.5 to 77.8 ms they cost before that work. The per-frame cost does not follow it and by arithmetic falls: the camera cap `geometry-off-frame-is-not-drawn` culls against is the frame's half-diagonal over the radius, the diagonal grows 8.3% while the radius grows 39.1%, so the cap narrows from 4.18/zoom to 3.26/zoom radians and a frame projects less geometry than it did. Two things were checked rather than assumed downstream: `subdivisionFade`'s 4.0 gate is derived from the stage's minimum and gets **more** room, because `LABEL_ROOM` is an absolute area and `screenArea` goes as the square of the scale, so Japan — the binding country — reaches its full name at 2.66x where it needed 3.7; and the ground under one pixel at the 32x ceiling goes from 1.03 km to 0.74, still inside what the served 1:10m outlines carry. Not measured in a browser: two sessions hold the dev ports, so every figure here is computed from the tokens and the code, and `routesScroll.test` computes the same sums so they fail rather than rot.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| the-plot-shows-no-tooltip                       | **The departure chart carries no SVG `<title>`, so a pointer resting on it is shown nothing.** The keyboard help stays in the document as the chart's `aria-describedby` and is unchanged.                                                                                                                                        | The owner asked for it about the flights: hovering a flight point painted five lines about arrow keys, plus and minus, zero and shift over the mark they were aiming at, and a tooltip that appears anywhere on a plot appears most often where a reader is trying to look. A `<title>` child is the only thing that draws a tooltip on an SVG — the attribute is accepted silently by JSX and never appears — so removing that one child is the whole of it. **Nothing accessible goes with it,** which is why this is a deletion rather than a trade: `HELP` was deliberately said in two places, and the other is the `srOnly` node the chart already points `aria-describedby` at, which is where a screen reader has always heard it. The `<title>` never was the chart's name either, since an `aria-label` beats it in the accessible-name calculation. Moving the help to a `<desc>` was the alternative and was rejected as a change with no reader: `<desc>` draws no tooltip and is not in the accessible-name or description path here, so it would have been a second copy nobody reads, and two copies of one sentence are what the constant exists to prevent. Leaving it and shortening it was rejected too — a shorter tooltip over the mark is still a tooltip over the mark. What is given up is that a reader with a pointer and no screen reader now learns the keys only from the line under the plot, which says “Point at the chart, or press an arrow key” and names no key beyond that. | a-flight-links-to-its-own-airline               | **Every flight links to a route-and-date search in its own airline's booking engine, never to an aggregator.** A carrier or an origin country we have no loaded URL for gets no link at all. The link is a mark beside the flight number, never the number itself, and it names a search and not a booking.                       | The owner wants a flight to reach the airline that flies it, and explicitly not Despegar, Google Flights or any aggregator. **The exact per-flight link does not exist to be built.** No booking URL appears anywhere in the provider's payload — the only carrier URLs in it are FAQ and baggage-policy pages — and the one token that does resolve to a booking resolves to a Google-hosted POST redirect, which is both an aggregator hop and a POST, so it could not be an `<a href>` even if the hop were acceptable. On the carriers' own sites there is nothing better waiting: none of the four takes a flight number in a URL, and three of them do not print flight numbers on the results page at all, because what they sell is a priced option bound to a shopping session that expires. So the reader is put on the same route on the same date in the airline's own engine and matches the departure by the clock — which the owner chose over no link at all. **The point of sale is the origin airport's country**, because LATAM's path needs a mandatory `/{country}/{language}/` segment with a slug written in that language and JetSMART needs a New Skies `cur` and `culture`; Aerolíneas needs neither, being one host in one country. What that gets wrong is recorded rather than hidden: it is the origin's country and not the reader's, so a Lima reader looking at SCL→AEP is quoted in Chilean pesos; the country arrives as the provider's own English name rather than as the ISO code sitting one field away from it upstream, so it is matched folded and unaccented; and an origin outside Peru, Chile and Argentina gets no LATAM and no JetSMART link, because both sell in Brazil and Colombia too and nobody here has loaded those storefronts' paths. **Avianca gets nothing** — 88 offers, about 2% of the archive, behind Akamai and never loaded cold — and nothing stands in its place, because 2% of rows quietly linking to a 404 costs more trust than 2% linking to nothing costs convenience. The link is its own small mark rather than the flight number turned into an anchor: as the anchor the number would have given the link the accessible name `LA 191`, a promise to open that one flight, and `.report` in `RouteList.module.css` already refuses text that reads as a fact and is not one. `searchLabel` writes `Search LATAM for LIM to CUZ on 12/09/2026` instead, which starts with a verb. **The scatter above gets none of these**: its ~899 marks are bare `<circle>` elements inside a chart that pans on a drag and tells a click from a drag by how far the pointer travelled, and a browser's own link activation would race that disambiguation on every press. And no dot-in-the-circle marker on the rows that have no link — the owner asked for one when links were expected to be rare, and a route-and-date search reaches about 98% of the archive's offers, so a marker is a decision to take with that number in front of them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| a-right-click-pins-the-reading                  | **A right-click on a mark in the departure chart pins the reading there**, so the crosshair, both plates, the readout and the spoken sentence stop following the pointer. `P` does the same from the keyboard; `Escape`, a pressed toggle above the plot and a second right-click all let it go.                                  | The owner: _"creo una accion para poder fijar la vista en un punto con anticlick"_. The reading followed the pointer and was lost the moment it moved, so a reader could not hold a fare beside anything — not the flight table under the plot, not another stretch of the frame. **What pins is the reading, and that settles what else does.** The hairlines, both plates, the marker, the line under the plot and the `role="status"` sentence are every one of them derived from a single `cursor` and from nothing else, so pinning is that value ceasing to be overwritten and the five stop together by construction. It is held as a flag beside the reading rather than as a copy of it, which is why a pinned flight takes its new price when a collection pass brings one: the pin names an itinerary and `resolve` re-finds it by key on every render, where a held copy would go on showing an hour-old fare. **The same mechanism answers every question about what it survives.** A zoom or a pan it survives, and more than survives — the crosshair is redrawn wherever that flight now sits and follows the mark. Being panned off the plot it does not, which is the rule this chart already keeps for everything a reader can point at or walk to: what is not on screen is not readable. A period step or a granularity change it does not, because every mark under it is a different mark; a route change it does not, because the component is unmounted by one. The pin is cleared while rendering rather than in an effect, so a frame showing a pin with nothing under it — this feature's own trap, committed by our own hand — is never painted. **Three ways out, because a state with no visible exit reads as a bug.** A pressed toggle beside the reset-zoom button is the discoverable one, always rendered and disabled when there is nothing to pin for the same reason its neighbour is; `Escape` is the one every reader already knows, and it only ever lets go, never pins; a second right-click on the same mark is convenient and is deliberately not the one this relies on, since nothing tells a reader that a gesture is a toggle. **`P` is the keyboard equivalent and `HELP` says so**: a pointer-only action in a chart that has two keyboard axes, a keyboard zoom and a spoken readout would be a regression rather than a feature. Enter and Space were rejected — Space scrolls the page from a focused element that is not a control, and Enter is what a reader expects to _open_ something. **The pinned state is said three ways** — the hairlines go solid where they were dashed, the readout gains the word `pinned`, and the button stays pressed — because a reading that looked identical held and live would have a reader take a stale fare for the current one. | one-pass-at-a-time-is-a-file                    | **One collection pass runs on this address at a time, across processes and not only inside one.** A pass takes a lock file before it plans and holds it until it is done; a pass that finds it held polls nothing and reports every departure as `another-pass-is-running`, in the same list and the same shape as `over-budget`. | The ledger bounds the day only _eventually_. `DailyBudget.spent()` re-reads the day file before every request, so a second spender is noticed within one request — but only once both passes have already planned. Two starting together each read a day with 600 left, each size a whole day's work against that, and each begin spending before either can see the other; `CollectionRunner`'s single slot serialises passes inside the API process and cannot see the scheduled command, which is a second process. **What is protected is planning-plus-spending, not the append.** A lock held only around `RequestLedger.spend` would serialise the writes and leave that arithmetic exactly where it was, and it would not buy the second thing either: `REQUEST_GAP_SECONDS` paces one loop, two loops halve it without anybody deciding to, and that is what 12.210 wanted and could only get inside one process. **Two locks and not one**, because the boards and the calendar are two slots on purpose: `calendar_job` records that a board pass is minutes long over dozens of departures and a calendar pass is two requests, so one shared lock would make a route added mid-board-pass go without the curve the horizon endpoint exists to fetch immediately — and it would decline rather than queue, which is worse than the case that row already rejected. Each slot is closed across processes and the open question about a shared _queue_ is left where it was. The day is safe either way, because only a board pass ever plans a whole day: a calendar pass allots one request per window per pair, checks what is left before each pair, and re-checks before every walk-back attempt. **Nothing blocks.** A pass is minutes long — a watched month is 31 departures three seconds apart — so a second one queueing behind it would be a scheduled task sitting on the machine for the length of the first, only to run against a day the first has already spent. Declining is instant, and it is reported rather than raised, because a cron firing while the owner presses Collect is the ordinary case and not a fault. **The mechanism is one atomic `O_EXCL` create, and it is the same one on both.** `fcntl.flock` does not exist on Windows, which is where this runs, and `msvcrt.locking` does not exist on Linux, which is where CI runs; either choice means two implementations of which the machine that matters would exercise one. What a file gives up against `flock` is the kernel's own liveness — a flock dies with its process and a file does not — so **a stale lock is timed against the silence, not against the work**: the holder refreshes it before every request it sends, the longest gap a living pass can produce is one paced wait plus one upstream timeout (3 + 12 seconds), and five minutes is twenty times that. Ageing the whole pass instead needs a bound of 600 requests times fifteen seconds — two and a half hours, ten missed passes on a fifteen-minute schedule, for a process killed at its first request. **Clearing one is a rename and not a delete**, which is what keeps the recovery from being a race of its own: “see that it is stale, then unlink” lets two processes both unlink, the second removing the lock the first has already replaced, while `os.replace` to a name only the caller knows can move a file away exactly once and the loser finds no source — and the winner still has to win the ordinary create, which is the one arbiter. The lock also names its holder, so a pass frozen long enough to look dead neither refreshes nor deletes the lock that replaced it. Measured 2026-08-21: six processes released at one wall-clock instant, six times over, gave exactly one winner cold and exactly one when all six saw the same stale lock. What separates the two is what they record: `fares/history/` and `fares/checks/` hold what the world cost, which exists nowhere else once the day passes, while this holds what **we** sent — and the heartbeats under `checks/` are never pruned, so the shape of an old day survives to within the look-to-request multiplier, exactly 1 for a board and the measured 2.43 for a calendar. | 2026-08-21 | Two passes can no longer both plan a whole day: a pass takes a lock file before it plans and holds it until it is done, and one that finds it held polls nothing and reports every departure as `another-pass-is-running` rather than raising — one lock for the boards and one for the calendar, so the two slots `calendar_job` argued for stay two and only a second pass of the same kind is turned away. It is an `O_EXCL` create, which behaves the same on Windows and in CI where `fcntl` and `msvcrt` each exist on only one of them; it goes stale after five minutes of silence rather than after the two and a half hours a whole pass may legitimately take, because the holder refreshes it before every request; and clearing one is a rename rather than a delete, so six processes racing one stale lock still leave exactly one winner. The spend ledger also stops growing forever — a day file is kept ninety days and swept when a new day opens, which is the only thing in this feature that is ever deleted and is separated from the append-only archive by recording what we sent rather than what the world cost (`one-pass-at-a-time-is-a-file`, `the-ledger-keeps-ninety-days`; S.40). |

No percentage anywhere, because 600 is a judgement and 329 is the only measured number in the pair. An unreadable ledger reads as `null` rather than zero and draws no bar at all. |
